brazil_caps_bite: National psychiatric admissions in Brazil fell by 41% between 2002 and 2016 (17.66 to 10.47 per 10,000), and the schizophrenia subset fell by 57% (7.97 to 3.43). This is a descriptive national trend — a fact about Brazil, not a causal claim about CAPS. It establishes that the inpatient margin the reform was meant to move did move, which is the first-order 'bite' the design needs. The reader should take away that something large happened on the outcome side of the reform's target, and that the series are close to monotone rather than a step at any single date.
brazil_caps_firstdiff_schiz: Within-municipality change in schizophrenia admissions after CAPS adoption, population-weighted to each state. Most states are negative; Rio Grande do Sul (+7.4) and Roraima (-7.0) are the largest movements in either direction, and Piauí and Rio de Janeiro fall least. The reader should take away that the national decline has real geography in it rather than being a uniform tide — which is what makes a staggered DiD informative here. Two limits: the teaching panel has no municipality map key, so this is drawn at the 27 states; and each state's colour is where its people are, not where its municipalities are.
brazil_caps_firstdiff_allmh: The same construction as the schizophrenia map, on all mental-disorder admissions. The pattern is similar and slightly more uniformly negative. Read beside the schizophrenia map, it says the reform's inpatient margin moved broadly, not only for the diagnosis the authors single out. The state-level and population-weighting caveats of the schizophrenia map apply identically.
brazil_caps_power: The design's minimum detectable effect is 0.1734 homicides per 10,000 (80% power, 5% two-sided), against an observed around-adoption change of 0.5238 unweighted and 0.5091 population-weighted. The MDE is 33% of that benchmark, so the design was capable of detecting a change a third the size of the raw movement — meaning a null would have been informative rather than merely inconclusive. Two caveats the reader should carry: the benchmark is an association, not the ATT, and the MDE is conservative because it is built for a single one-year contrast while the CS-DiD averages many group-time cells.
pscore_main: Estimated probability of ever adopting a CAPS, probit on the 13 baseline covariates in the 2002 cross-section. The never-treated (outline) and ever-treated (filled) distributions overlap substantially: 0 controls have a propensity score above 0.995, and the supports overlap rather than separating. The reader should take away that common support holds, so no trimming was applied and none needed to be. This is the one balance diagnostic that passed cleanly — the level-balance table did not, with all 13 covariates exceeding the |0.25| normalized-difference threshold.
rollout_panelview: Which municipalities are treated in each year, ordered by adoption timing. Adoptions begin in 2003, peak at 216 municipalities in 2006, and continue through 2016, with 3,836 municipalities never adopting and 296 already treated in the first panel year. The reader should take away that this is a genuinely staggered rollout with a long tail of late adopters, which is exactly the structure that makes two-way fixed effects with already-treated controls a biased estimator and Callaway-Sant'Anna the appropriate choice.
outcome_by_cohort: Mean homicides per 10,000 by adoption cohort, with each cohort's line stopping at the year before it adopts. Post-adoption years are excluded on purpose: this is a comparability check, and looking at the after-period here would turn it into an early peek at the answer. Levels differ across cohorts — adopters are not a random draw, consistent with all 13 covariates failing the balance threshold — but the pre-period slopes are broadly parallel and none is flat. The reader should take away that the design's parallel-trends requirement is not obviously violated and not obviously satisfied. Two things to notice: the never-treated line rises throughout, and the 2003 cohort has a single pre-year, so its pre-trend cannot be assessed at all — the same cohort that failed the EPV screen at 3.62.
csdid_event_study_main: Callaway-Sant'Anna event study for homicides, not-yet-treated comparison, 13 covariates, 95% uniform bands. The pre-treatment leads at -5 to -2 are small and every band covers zero. After adoption the estimates rise, reaching +0.22 per 10,000 at four to five years. THE THING TO NOTICE: the sign is POSITIVE — adoption is associated with more homicides — which is the opposite of the published result this panel comes from. That discrepancy is unreconciled and is flagged in the stage findings rather than smoothed over. The reader should take away that the pre-trend evidence is reassuring, the post-treatment estimate is not null, and the direction disagrees with the paper, so the number should not be quoted as a replication.
csdid_event_study_falsif: The same sample, the same 13 covariates and the same estimator settings as the main run, on deaths of despair per 10,000 instead of homicides. The simple placebo ATT is -0.0145 (SE 0.0355, p = 0.684) and every event-time band covers zero, pre and post. The reader should take away that whatever is moving homicides is not moving an outcome the reform has no identified channel into — the design is not simply picking up a differential trend shared by everything. Two honest limits: sim_overdose is 96.8% zeros so this rests on sim_diseases_despair, and deaths of despair are not an unrelated outcome, so this is evidence against a generic trend artifact rather than evidence of no mental-health effect.
